newsitem.title: USA: Apple to cut back severance pay, sabbaticals.
newsitem.headline: Apple to cut back severance pay, sabbaticals.

text.p: Apple Computer Inc. co-founder Steve Jobs sent a memo to employees saying the ailing personal computer maker will cut back on severance pay for laid-off employees, curtail its generous sabbatical program and limit business travel to essential trips.
Apple's board of directors also approved more stock options for employees as an incentive to turn the company's fortunes around, Jobs said.

"Today we are taking a few more steps which will begin to take Apple back to its roots as a more egalitarian, entrepreneurial company," Jobs wrote in an internal electronic message dated Aug. 12 that was obtained by Reuters.
The memo was signed "Steve and the executive committee."

The move by Jobs -- who is now on the board but has said he is not interested in running Apple again -- is the latest in his attempts to rescue the Cupertino, Calif.-based company he co-founded in 1976. Even though Jobs is not a formal executive at Apple, he is playing a big role in running its day-to-day operations. Apple has just under 10,000 employees worldwide.
"It makes perfect sense to me. He wants Apple to start thinking again like a high-tech start-up," Lou Mazzucchelli, a Gerard Klauer & Mattison analyst, said of Jobs' latest attempts to revive Apple.

"I think he has always been upset that the company turned into this bloated bureaucratic organization," Mazzucchelli said. "He is using his informal authority as founder of the company, and I'm sure he is doing it with the blessing of the board."
The moves have been approved by Apple's executive committee, which is running the company until a new chief executive and chairman are found.
Apple is narrowing down candidates to replace Gilbert Amelio, who was ousted by the board a month ago as CEO, a source familiar with the search said.
The source said there are 10 to 20 executives in the world who are qualified and willing to take the position. Apple said last week that it expects the search to be completed within three months.

Jobs and pal Steve Wozniak created Apple 22 years ago in Jobs' parents' garage. For much of the 1980s under Jobs' influence, the company was a trendsetter in giving generous benefits to employees as an incentive to create innovative computers.
Jobs was ousted as chairman in 1985 but returned to the company after Apple bought his company, Next Software Inc., last December.

Since the board ousted Amelio as chairman and CEO last month, Jobs essentially has been running Apple, even though his full-time job is chairman and CEO of Pixar Animation Studios, creator of the hit movie "Toy Story."

He also was instrumental in a deal that shocked the computer industry last week. Microsoft Corp. agreed to invest $150 million in Apple and promised to continue writing software for the Macintosh, which provided a huge psychological boost to Apple's prospects.

"The bottom line is, he is trying to get everyone to understand that it's "nose-to-the-grindstone time," said Tim Bajarin, president of consultancy Creative Strategies Inc. in San Jose, Calif. "Even though they had some significant announcements last week, they are nowhere out of the woods yet."

On Monday, in its quarterly filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Apple said it expects to report a loss for the fiscal fourth-quarter ending in September and also said sales will be lower than the year-ago period. The company also said it does not believe it will return to profitability in the fourth quarter.

Investors seem to like Jobs' moves in the past month, judging by Apple recent stock price. The stock rose 94 cents to $23 at mid-afternoon on Nasdaq, more than 60 percent higher than a month ago when the stock traded near $14.
